items.s: Finances a public library that charges patrons no fees.
items.w: GO bonds fund non-revenue-producing facilities that serve the whole community, such as libraries and parks.

items.s: Debt service is paid solely from the tolls collected on the bridge it financed.
items.w: Revenue bonds are repaid from the stream of income generated by the financed project, not from taxes.

items.s: Many new issues must first pass a voter bond referendum.
items.w: Voter approval through a bond referendum applies to GO bonds, while it does not apply to revenue bonds.

items.s: Can be issued outside the issuer’s legislative debt limits because taxes do not back it.
items.w: Revenue bonds are not tax-backed, so statutory debt limits on outstanding GO principal do not restrict them.

items.s: Backed by the issuer’s full faith and credit and its full taxing power.
items.w: GO bonds are guaranteed by revenues raised primarily from the issuer’s taxing authority, per the book.

items.s: The issuer has no obligation to pay from any source except the revenues specifically pledged.
items.w: A revenue bond issuer is not obligated beyond the pledged project revenues, unlike a GO issuer.

items.s: Property tax computed on assessed value is the most common source of repayment.
items.w: Ad valorem property taxes are the most common source used to redeem GO bond issues.

items.s: Arises when mortgage rates fall and homeowners refinance.
items.w: Falling rates give homeowners a reason to prepay and refinance at a lower rate.

items.s: Arises when mortgage rates rise and homeowners keep their existing loans.
items.w: Rising rates remove any reason to refinance, so mortgages stay outstanding longer than expected.

items.s: The MBS effective maturity shortens, much like a bond being called.
items.w: Prepaid mortgages leave the pool early, so the MBS behaves like a callable bond with shorter life.

items.s: The MBS effective maturity lengthens beyond what the investor originally anticipated.
items.w: As prepayment speeds decline, the mortgages remain outstanding longer and the MBS maturity is extended.

items.s: Investors receive principal back early and must reinvest at lower rates.
items.w: Early return of principal in a falling-rate market creates reinvestment rate risk for the MBS holder.

items.s: Price drops significantly because a long-term bond is extremely sensitive to rising rates.
items.w: The extended MBS acts like a long-term bond, so higher rates cut its price substantially.

items.s: The MBS price shows no real increase despite lower rates, as it acts like a short-term security.
items.w: Shortened maturity makes the MBS less sensitive to rate declines, so its market value does not rise.

items.s: The bid quote is higher than the ask quote.
items.w: Bills are quoted on a discount basis, so a higher discount for the buyer means a lower price.

items.s: The ask quote is higher than the bid quote.
items.w: For notes and bonds the ask price is always higher than the bid price, and the difference is the spread.

items.s: Quoted as an annualized discount from face value using a 360-day year.
items.w: T-bills are quoted on a discounted yield basis, expressed as an annual rate on a 360-day year.

items.s: Quoted as a percentage of par in 32nds of a point.
items.w: T-notes and T-bonds are quoted in 32nds, for example 95:07 equals a price of 95 7/32 percent.

items.s: Pays no periodic interest; sold at a discount and matures at par.
items.w: Bills behave like zero-coupon bonds, so the investor’s return is the difference between price and par.

items.s: Pays interest every six months until maturity.
items.w: T-notes and T-bonds both pay semiannual interest, unlike bills which pay only at maturity through the discount.

items.s: Issued with a maximum maturity of 52 weeks.
items.w: Bills mature in one year or less, with 4, 13, 26 and 52 week maturities.

items.s: A debt security issued outside the United States but denominated in US dollars.
items.w: A Eurodollar bond is issued abroad, for example in Argentina, yet is denominated in dollars.

items.s: US dollars held in an account at a bank in Switzerland.
items.w: US dollars held in a bank overseas are called a Eurodollar deposit, per the Knopman Note.

items.s: Not registered with the SEC and trades outside the United States.
items.w: Eurodollar bonds are issued and trade outside the US and are not registered with the SEC.

items.s: Issuers use it to be more marketable when their home currency is unstable.
items.w: A borrower with an unstable home currency sells dollar-denominated bonds to attract investors.

items.s: Does not involve a borrower issuing a security to investors; it is simply dollars held abroad.
items.w: A deposit is a bank balance in dollars outside the US, not a bond issued by a borrower.

items.s: Transferable to other investors, so it is considered a security.
items.w: Because negotiable CDs can be transferred, they are securities that can trade in the secondary market.

items.s: Cannot be resold and can only be redeemed by the issuing bank.
items.w: Non-negotiable CDs are redeemable only through the issuing bank and cannot be sold to other investors.

items.s: Has a minimum face value of $100,000.
items.w: The book gives a $100,000 minimum face value for negotiable CDs, unlike retail CDs.

items.s: Not considered a security and does not trade in the money market.
items.w: Since they cannot be traded, non-negotiable CDs are not securities and stay out of the money market.

items.s: Can be sold in a secondary market, though that market is often quite limited.
items.w: Negotiable CDs trade in the secondary market, but liquidity there tends to be limited.

items.s: The type of CD most commonly offered to individual retail customers.
items.w: Most CDs offered to individuals are non-negotiable, which means they cannot be resold.

items.s: Counts as a money market security, and many carry maturities of one year or less.
items.w: Negotiable CDs are money market securities, with many maturing in one year or less.

title: Public purpose vs private activity munis

items.s: Finances a public school building, so interest is federally tax-exempt.
items.w: Public purpose bonds, which benefit the municipality at large, pay federally tax-exempt interest.

items.s: Finances a stadium, so interest may not qualify for the federal tax exemption.
items.w: Stadium and similar financings provide little public benefit and are private activity issues that may be taxable.

items.s: Industrial development revenue bond whose proceeds build a plant leased to a corporation.
items.w: IDR bonds benefit a private company and are considered private activity bonds, backed by its lease payments.

items.s: The immediate benefit goes to the community at large rather than to a single company.
items.w: Public purpose bonds benefit the municipality at large, unlike private activity bonds whose benefit belongs to a private company.

items.s: Interest on certain bonds of this type is included in the alternative minimum tax calculation.
items.w: The AMT calculation includes interest on private activity bonds, as shown on the official statement cover.

items.s: Resident buying the in-state bond pays no federal or state income tax on interest.
items.w: Public purpose bonds from the investor’s own state are free of federal and state income taxes.

items.s: Credit quality depends mainly on lease payments from the borrowing corporation.
items.w: IDR debt is the responsibility of the corporation, so its credit quality drives the bond’s credit quality.
